prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, reaching 10^-18 fractional uncertainty and opening new tests of fundamental physics and a path to redefining the second

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a well-bounded invention with a clear originating idea: Katori's magic-wavelength trapping removes Doppler and recoil shifts while keeping a large number of atoms, which is what allows both low systematic uncertainty and high stability. Ye's group then took strontium lattice clocks to the 10^-18 level and into many-body clock physics. Four of the eight members ranked it in their top three and six ranked it at all, and every member who ranked it proposed the same two names, so there is no attribution dispute inside this committee. Independent laboratories reproduce the performance and intercompare clocks, so the result is not tied to one group. Its consequences are concrete: tests of the constancy of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy through the gravitational redshift at centimetre scale, and the international discussion on redefining the second. It is a clear case where improved measurement opens new physics, and the underlying physics (laser cooling, trapping, narrow-line spectroscopy) is atomic physics that I can judge directly.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is proximity to earlier prizes: the 2005 award for laser-based precision spectroscopy and the frequency comb, and the 2012 award for ion control and ion clocks. A reader could say the lattice clock is a refinement of an already honoured line of work, and that the prize would be better waited out until the redefinition of the second actually takes place. There is also an incomplete-credit question, since Yb lattice clocks, Al+ ion clocks and the groups at SYRTE, PTB and NIST reached comparable accuracy and are not named. My view is that the magic-wavelength idea and the 10^-18 demonstration are a separate, identifiable step and that the redefinition is a consequence rather than the merit, but I accept that the committee could weigh this differently.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked the lattice clock first with me, but asked whether it should be paired with the Hall and Hansch comb work already recognised in 2005, and whether the ion-clock prize of 2012 blurs the claim.
responses.response: I agree on the first point and disagree with a pairing. The comb is the readout tool and was honoured as such; the lattice clock's own novelty is the magic-wavelength trap that makes a many-atom, Doppler-free optical standard possible. Adding comb names would reintroduce credit that is already settled and would push the configuration past the clean two-name set that you and I both proposed. On the ion clocks, a single-ion clock and a many-atom lattice clock differ in how they trade statistics against systematics, so I treat them as sibling achievements rather than the same one. I do share your caution that the distinction must be written into the citation explicitly.

responses.point: Pearce ranked the gamma-ray burst afterglow discovery first as a clear, observation-driven result, and placed the lattice clock third, noting overlap with earlier prizes for spectroscopy and ion manipulation and that the redefinition of the second is not itself evidence of merit.
responses.response: I accept your last point and have not argued from the redefinition; the case rests on the 10^-18 performance and what it already delivered. I take the afterglow discovery seriously as a candidate, but I have two concerns that make me hesitate to place it first. The names supplied omit Jan van Paradijs and the optical-identification teams, which you flagged yourself, and I cannot say how X-ray localisation and optical redshift should be divided. By contrast, the lattice clock attribution is not contested among us. I also do not find the earlier-prize argument decisive: Hall and Hansch were honoured for the comb and Wineland for single-ion control, neither for the lattice scheme.

responses.point: Johansson ranked trapped-ion quantum computing first (Cirac, Zoller, Blatt), arguing that it is mature, foundational for quantum-information hardware, and that Wineland's 2012 prize covered ion control and not the gate proposals.
responses.response: I ranked B018 second and it is my first alternative, so I take the case seriously. Our disagreement is on overlap and on credit. The 2012 prize recognised the control of single quantum systems, which is precisely the toolbox on which the Cirac-Zoller gate and Blatt's experiments rest, so the committee would need a clear argument that the gate proposal is a separate step. The experimental credit is also thin: the first ion gate came out of the NIST group and Monroe, who are not among the credited names, so a Blatt-only experimental side is narrower than the history. I would not rule out your configuration, but it looks to me more exposed to attribution objections than the clock.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked the experimental discovery of the Higgs boson first, crediting the founders of ATLAS and CMS, and argued that recognition is overdue and that the 2013 prize covered only the theory.
responses.response: I agree the discovery is of the first importance and that it is mature. My difficulty is the attribution rather than the science. Two collaborations of several thousand people, and a prize naming three founders and spokespeople, rewards conception and construction leadership and not the discovery analysis, and you acknowledge yourself that other leaders could be argued with equal force. I cannot see that this is resolved by the supplied names. I would rather be told what principle the committee uses to pick three people from that field, because without it I would not give it priority over a candidate with a clean credit set.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as a distinct step relative to the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which is a judgement the written citation has to support.
Whether to wait for the actual redefinition of the second, or whether the 10^-18 demonstrations already suffice.
Credit for the ytterbium lattice and aluminium-ion clock groups that reached comparable accuracy and are outside the two names.
No resolution on the credit questions in B018 and B004 (Monroe and NIST; Girvin versus Blais), which affects how strongly I would back either as a fallback.
statement.conflict_note: A possible perceived connection that may require recusal discussion: my profile records a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Jun Ye's career is tied to the Hall/JILA environment. The profile documents no direct collaboration, supervision or shared funding with Ye or Katori, so I flag the connection for the committee to judge and do not claim a specific conflict. I also have a field-level proximity to the AMO candidates (B018, B004, B044) as an atomic physicist and Lund colleague of the quantum-information community, and that bears on how the committee should weigh my views on them.
